claim: Neural crest cells delaminate from the neural tube to engage in extensive migration throughout the embryo.
source: Neural crest cells delaminate from the neural tube to engage in extensive migration throughout the embryo (Figure 1a–b).
evidence: This is stated directly in the text and supported by Figure 1a-b showing neural crest migration.

claim: As neural crest cells move away from the neural tube, they undergo drastic changes in their transcriptional identity, and transition from multipotent progenitors to committed cell types.
source: As these cells move away from the neural tube, they undergo drastic changes in their transcriptional identity, and transition from multipotent progenitors to committed cell types.
evidence: This is directly stated in the manuscript text.

claim: The formation and differentiation of the neural crest is controlled by a complex gene regulatory network, composed by multiple signaling pathways, transcription factors, and epigenetic modifiers.
source: The formation and differentiation of the neural crest is controlled by a complex gene regulatory network, composed by multiple signaling pathways, transcription factors, and epigenetic modifiers (Simões-Costa and Bronner, 2015; Meulemans and Bronner-Fraser, 2004; Betancur et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Expression of the early components of the neural crest gene regulatory network defines the neural crest stem cell population that resides within the dorsal neural tube.
source: Expression of the early components of this network defines the neural crest stem cell population that resides within the dorsal neural tube (Lignell et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lignell et al., 2017.

claim: The early gene regulatory network includes neural crest markers and pluripotency factors such as Pax7, FoxD3, Ets1, Myc, and Sox5.
source: This set of genes, which includes neural crest markers and pluripotency factors, endows the neural crest stem cells with their unique features, such as multipotency and self-renewal.
evidence: The text mentions these genes as part of the early network that maintains multipotency.

claim: Lin28a is strongly enriched in neural crest cells during specification.
source: Isolation of neural crest with the Tfap2aE1 and RT-PCR quantitation showed strong enrichment of Lin28a mRNA during specification (Figure 1—figure supplement 1q).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1q.

claim: Lin28b is expressed at much lower levels than Lin28a and is not enriched in neural crest cells.
source: This was not observed for the other Lin28 gene present in the chick genome, Lin28b (Tsialikas and Romer-Seibert, 2015). The paralog was expressed at much lower levels and was not enriched in neural crest cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1q–r).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1q-r and a citation.

claim: There is a marked reduction in Lin28a mRNA levels at later stages of neural crest development, concomitant with silencing of neural crest stem cell genes.
source: Interestingly, there was a marked reduction in Lin28a mRNA levels at later stages, concomitant with silencing of the neural crest stem cell genes (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Lin28a is dynamically expressed during neural crest development and is most abundant in premigratory cells that reside within the neural tube.
source: These results show that Lin28a is dynamically expressed during neural crest development, and that it is most abundant in premigratory cells that reside within the neural tube.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the expression data presented.

claim: Sustained expression of Lin28a maintains expression of neural crest stem cell factors at stages when these genes would normally be downregulated.
source: This analysis revealed that migratory cells constitutively expressing Lin28a maintained expression of neural crest stem cell factors even at stages when these genes would normally be downregulated (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Maintenance of early neural crest factors by Lin28a overexpression results in a delay in differentiation.
source: This maintenance of early neural crest factors resulted in a delay in differentiation, as evidenced by a decrease in the expression of ectomesenchymal, neuronal and glial markers in late migrating cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2i).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2i.

claim: Loss of Lin28a results in decreased expression of neural crest markers FoxD3 and Sox10.
source: Loss of Lin28a resulted in decreased expression of neural crest markers FoxD3 and Sox10, as shown by immunohistochemistry (Figure 1g–i) and in situ hybridization (Figure 1—figure supplement 3e–h).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry and in situ hybridization data shown in multiple figures.

claim: The phenotype of Lin28a knockdown is not due to changes in cell cycle exit or cell death.
source: Immunohistochemistry for phospho-histone H3 and Caspase-3 confirmed that this phenotype was not due to changes in cell cycle exit or cell death (Figure 1—figure supplement 4a–c,f–g).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockdown of Lin28a results in a significant reduction in the number of FoxD3 and Sox10 positive cells.
source: Consistent with the morpholino experiments, targeting the first exon of Lin28a with a pair of gRNAs resulted in a significant reduction in the number of FoxD3 and Sox10 positive cells (Figure 1k–l, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by CRISPR/Cas9 data shown in Figure 1k-l.

claim: DsiRNA-mediated knockdown of Lin28a, but not Lin28b, results in a significant decrease in the expression of FoxD3 and Sox10.
source: Finally, DsiRNA-mediated knockdown of Lin28a, but not of Lin28b, resulted in a significant decrease in the expression of FoxD3 and Sox10 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3n–o).
evidence: This is supported by DsiRNA knockdown data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3n-o.

claim: Knockdown of Lin28a results in dispersed ganglia with abnormal condensation and a marked reduction in the maxillomandibular lobe of the trigeminal ganglion.
source: Immunohistochemistry with neuronal marker Tuj1 revealed that knockdown of Lin28a resulted in dispersed ganglia with abnormal condensation. In particular, we observed a marked reduction in the maxillomandibular lobe of the trigeminal ganglion (Figure 1—figure supplement 4j–o).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4j-o.

claim: High levels of Lin28a during early development are necessary for neural crest specification.
source: Taken together, these functional experiments indicate that high levels of Lin28a during early development are necessary for neural crest specification, while its subsequent downregulation is required for silencing of progenitor identity.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the functional experiments described.

claim: Lin28a is a bona fide pluripotency factor that has been shown to underlie stemness and to drive reprogramming of somatic cells.
source: Lin28a is a bona fide pluripotency factor that has been shown to underlie stemness and to drive reprogramming of somatic cells (Yu et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Transfection with a Lin28a expression vector results in a six-fold increase in multipotent neural crest cells.
source: Quantification of cell types in colonies from the control and experimental groups revealed a six-fold increase in multipotent (that generated four or more cell types) neural crest cells after transfection with a Lin28a expression vector (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is supported by single-cell clonal analysis data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Mock-transfected neural crest cells are biased towards a glial fate (60% of the total progeny).
source: Furthermore, while mock-transfected neural crest cells were biased towards a glial fate (60% of the total progeny), the experimental group had a more uniform distribution of derivatives (Figure 2e, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by single-cell clonal analysis data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Lin28a overexpression results in a larger percentage of multipotent progenitors compared to the control group.
source: Consistent with this, classification of neural crest progenitors according to their developmental potentials revealed a larger percentage of multipotent progenitors (like GCMS progenitors, which give rise to glia, chondroblasts, melanocytes and smooth muscles), when compared to the control group (Figure 2f, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by single-cell clonal analysis data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: Changes in Lin28a levels affect specific properties of neural crest cells, such as their ability to give rise to multiple cell types.
source: The results from this single-cell clonal analysis indicate that the changes in the transcriptional network observed following manipulation in the Lin28a levels affect specific properties of neural crest cells, such as their ability to give rise to multiple cell types.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the single-cell clonal analysis.

claim: Lin28a regulates genes post-transcriptionally both directly by binding to mRNAs, or indirectly by inhibiting maturation of the let-7 family of microRNAs.
source: Lin28a has been shown to regulate genes post-transcriptionally both directly by binding to mRNAs, or indirectly by inhibiting maturation of the let-7 family of microRNAs, which are potent post-transcriptional repressors (Newman et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Newman et al., 2008.

claim: Neural crest stem cells have low let-7 activity, which continuously increases as the cells migrate away from the neural tube.
source: By transfecting embryos with the sensor, we observed that although neural crest stem cells have low let-7 activity, it continuously increases as the cells migrate away from the neural tube (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by let-7 sensor data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: There is a significant increase in the expression levels of let-7 miRNAs from the premigratory (HH8) to the late-migrating (HH12) neural crest.
source: Consistent with this, RT-PCR analysis revealed a significant increase in the expression levels of let-7 miRNAs from the premigratory (HH8) to the late-migrating (HH12) neural crest (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: In the absence of Lin28a, let-7 activity increases.
source: The results show that in the absence of Lin28a, let-7 activity increased, as evidenced by a reduction in let-7 sensor expression (Figure 3d–e) and direct measurement of multiple mature let-7s through RT-PCR (Figure 3f, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by let-7 sensor and RT-PCR data shown in Figures 3d-f.

claim: Transfection with a let-7a mimic molecule results in loss of FoxD3+ cells and reduced expression of neural crest markers.
source: Furthermore, transfection with a let-7a mimic molecule resulted in loss of FoxD3 +cells (Figure 3g–h) and reduced the expression of neural crest markers (Figure 3i), recapitulating the phenotype of Lin28a knockdown.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry and RT-PCR data shown in Figures 3g-i.

claim: Let-7a mimic treatment does not alter proliferation or cell death.
source: This treatment did not alter proliferation or cell death, as evidenced by immunostaining with pH3 and Caspase-3 antibodies, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 4d–e,h–i).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4d-e,h-i.

claim: Wild-type Lin28a protein can rescue the loss of neural crest caused by Lin28a knockdown.
source: The wild-type Lin28a protein was able to rescue the loss of neural crest; however, the mCCHC Lin28a mutant protein could not restore FoxD3 or Sox10 expression.
evidence: This is supported by epistatic experiments described in the text.

claim: The mCCHC Lin28a mutant protein, which cannot bind to let-7 miRNAs, cannot rescue the loss of neural crest caused by Lin28a knockdown.
source: The wild-type Lin28a protein was able to rescue the loss of neural crest; however, the mCCHC Lin28a mutant protein could not restore FoxD3 or Sox10 expression.
evidence: This is supported by epistatic experiments described in the text.

claim: Transfection with a let-7 sponge construct recapitulates the wild-type Lin28a rescue of neural crest loss.
source: Furthermore, transfection with a let-7 sponge construct, which reduces the levels of free mature let-7, recapitulated the wild-type Lin28a rescue (Figure 3k–l, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by epistatic experiments shown in Figures 3k-l.

claim: Lin28a regulates neural crest genes via the let-7 dependent pathway.
source: These results indicate that Lin28a regulates neural crest genes via the let-7 dependent pathway, and suggest that let-7 miRNAs mediate the silencing of neural crest genes observed during late migration (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the epistatic experiments.

claim: Inhibition of let-7 activity results in maintenance of Pax7, FoxD3, Sox5, cMyc, and Ets1 in late neural crest cells.
source: RT-PCR analysis revealed that this inhibition of let-7 activity results in maintenance of Pax7, FoxD3, Sox5, cMyc, and Ets1, recapitulating the effect of Lin28a overexpression (Figure 1e, Figure 3m).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3m.

claim: Lin28a is itself a let-7 target, and these factors form a double-negative feedback loop.
source: Consistent with published data showing that Lin28a is itself a let-7 target (Rybak et al., 2008), and that these factors form a double-negative feedback loop, we also detected higher levels of the pluripotency factor in these cells (Figure 3m).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data in Figure 3m and a citation to Rybak et al., 2008.

claim: Neural crest stem cell identity is regulated by the Lin28a/let-7 axis.
source: Taken together, these experiments indicate that neural crest stem cell identity is regulated by the Lin28a/let-7 axis, consistent with the possibility that the balance between these two factors underlies the collapse of the multipotency network observed during differentiation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experiments described.

claim: Lin28a loss-of-function and let-7 gain-of-function recapitulate the changes that occur in late migratory neural crest cells.
source: Both Lin28a loss- and let-7 gain-of-function recapitulated the changes that occur in late migratory neural crest cells (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is supported by Nanostring analysis comparing different conditions.

claim: Neural crest genes are strongly down-regulated in both Lin28a loss-of-function and let-7 gain-of-function treatments.
source: By comparing control and targeted cells from individual embryos, we found that neural crest genes were strongly down-regulated in both treatments, suggesting that premature let-7 activity has a systemic effect on the neural crest gene regulatory network (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is supported by Nanostring data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Genes that modulate neural crest multipotency, such as Sox10, FoxD3, Sox5, Ets1, and cMyc, are particularly susceptible to changes in the Lin28a/let-7 balance.
source: Furthermore, genes that have been reported to modulate neural crest multipotency, such as Sox10, FoxD3, Sox5, Ets1, and cMyc, were particularly susceptible to changes in the Lin28a/let-7 balance (Figure 4d, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by Nanostring data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: The Lin28a/let-7 axis regulates neural crest development by modulating the entire transcriptional network.
source: These results indicate the Lin28a/let-7 axis regulates neural crest development by modulating the entire transcriptional network.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the Nanostring analysis.

claim: Increased let-7 activity suppresses multipotency and stemness in neural crest progenitors.
source: Furthermore, the striking loss of stem cell genes (Lignell et al., 2017) observed in these experiments indicates that increased let-7 activity suppresses multipotency and stemness in neural crest progenitors.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the Nanostring analysis and a citation to Lignell et al., 2017.

claim: The 3' UTRs of FoxD3, Pax7, and Myc show decreased activity when co-transfected with let-7 mimic.
source: The 3' UTR reporters for FoxD3, Pax7, and Myc (Figure 4i–j; Figure 4—figure supplement 1c,f), which have let-7 target sites (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a), showed decreased activity when they were co-transfected with the let-7 mimic.
evidence: This is supported by UTR-reporter assay data shown in Figures 4i-j and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The 3' UTR reporters for Sox10, Sox8 and Zic1, which lack let-7 target sites, are unaffected by let-7 gain-of-function.
source: In contrast, the reporters for Sox10, Sox8 and Zic1 UTRs, which lack target sites for the microRNAs, were unaffected by the gain-of-function assay (Figure 4j, Figure 4—figure supplement 1b,d–e).
evidence: This is supported by UTR-reporter assay data shown in Figure 4j and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: FoxD3 protein expression rapidly decreases during migration, while enhancer activity does not significantly change.
source: We found that FoxD3 protein expression rapidly decreased during migration, while enhancer activity did not significantly change between neural crest cells close to the neural tube and those that had further migrated out (Figure 4—figure supplement 1g–j).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and enhancer reporter data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1g-j.

claim: Post-transcriptional regulation is necessary for timely silencing of components of the gene regulatory network.
source: This indicates that post-transcriptional regulation, which is absent from the enhancer construct, is necessary for timely silencing of components of the gene regulatory network.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of FoxD3 protein and enhancer activity.

claim: Targeting of individual let-7 sites in the Pax7 and FoxD3 loci results in a mild but consistent increase in the expression of these genes at stages when they are normally downregulated.
source: Targeting of individual let-7 sites in both the Pax7 and FoxD3 loci resulted in a mild but consistent increase in the expression of these genes (Figure 4k), at the stages that they are normally downregulated; a control gRNA (gRNA4) targeting a region of the FoxD3 UTR devoid of let-7 miRNAs sites had no effect on gene expression.
evidence: This is supported by CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing data shown in Figure 4k.

claim: Let-7 miRNAs orchestrate the silencing of progenitor cell identity by directly repressing critical network nodes.
source: These results indicate that let-7 miRNAs orchestrate the silencing of progenitor cell identity by directly repressing critical network nodes (Figure 4i).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the UTR-reporter and CRISPR experiments.

claim: Inhibitory interactions from let-7 propagate in a domino-like fashion throughout the network, resulting in its collapse.
source: We speculate that these inhibitory interactions propagate in a domino-like fashion throughout the network, resulting in its collapse (Figure 4l).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the data.

claim: ATAC-seq performed in sorted neural crest cells revealed eleven non-coding regions of open chromatin in the Lin28a locus.
source: Assay for Transposase-Accessible Chromatin (ATAC-seq) performed in sorted neural crest cells revealed eleven non-coding regions of open chromatin in the Lin28a locus (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Only one region of open chromatin, located in the second intron of Lin28a (Lin28E1), was able to drive reporter activity in the neural crest and ectoderm.
source: Transient transgenesis experiments in chick embryos showed that only one of these regions, located in the second intron of Lin28a (Lin28E1) (Figure 5a, Figure 5—figure supplement 1b) was able to drive reporter activity in the neural crest and ectoderm (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is supported by transient transgenesis data shown in Figures 5a-b and Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The Lin28E1 enhancer sequence contains four TCF/LEF binding sites, suggesting regulation by canonical Wnt signaling.
source: The sequence of this enhancer, which is conserved in amniotes, contains four TCF/LEF binding sites (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c), suggesting regulation by canonical Wnt signaling.
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Lin28a protein expression is strongest in the dorsal neural tube, a known source of Wnt ligands.
source: Consistent with this, Lin28a protein expression was strongest in the dorsal neural tube, a known source of Wnt ligands (Simões-Costa et al., 2015; Hollyday et al., 1995) (Figure 5c–d).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figures 5c-d and citations.

claim: Mutation of the four TCF/LEF binding sites in Lin28E1 results in complete loss of enhancer activity specifically in neural crest cells.
source: This resulted in complete loss of enhancer activity specifically in neural crest cells (Figure 5e–f), and also prevented enhancer association with Wnt-effector Lef1 in enhancer pull-down experiments (Figure 5g).
evidence: This is supported by enhancer reporter and pull-down data shown in Figures 5e-g.

claim: Disruption of Wnt signaling using morpholinos targeting Wnt1 and Wnt4 reduces expression of both endogenous Lin28a and Lin28E1 activity.
source: Second, we conducted loss-of-function experiments by disrupting Wnt signaling using morpholinos targeting two Wnt ligands expressed in the dorsal neural folds, Wnt1 and Wnt4 (Simões-Costa et al., 2015). This knockdown reduced expression of both endogenous Lin28a and Lin28E1 activity (Figure 5h).
evidence: This is supported by morpholino knockdown data shown in Figure 5h and a citation.

claim: Loss of Wnt signaling results in increased levels of mature let-7s.
source: Moreover, loss of Wnt signaling resulted in increased levels of mature let-7s (Figure 5h).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5h.

claim: Lef1 and nuclear β-catenin (Ctnnb1) are associated with Lin28E1 in neural crest cells.
source: Finally, chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) revealed that Lef1 and nuclear b-catenin (Ctnnb1) are associated with Lin28E1 in neural crest cells, indicating that canonical Wnts are directly regulating Lin28a.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data described in the text.

claim: The interaction between Lef1/β-catenin and Lin28E1 is dependent on Wnt activity.
source: This interaction is dependent on Wnt activity, as binding to the enhancer was lost in embryos transfected with a Wnt1 dominant negative construct (Figure 5i).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 5i.

claim: Neural crest cells exhibit a reduction in Wnt-activation and an increase in let-7 activity as they migrate away from the neural tube.
source: Consistent with our prediction, the analysis revealed a decrease in Wnt activity and increased let-7 mediated repression during migration (Figure 5k–l, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by single-cell analysis data shown in Figures 5k-l.

claim: The topological relationship between a neural crest cell and the Wnt niche determines the balance of Lin28a/let-7 activity, which in turn modulates the early transcriptional network.
source: Based on these results, we propose that the topological relationship between a neural crest cell and the Wnt niche determines the balance of Lin28a/let-7 activity, which in turn modulates the early transcriptional network.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data.

claim: Migrating neural crest cells constitutively expressing Wnt1 have higher levels of Lin28a and lower let-7 activity.
source: As predicted, we found that migrating neural crest cells constitutively expressing Wnt1 have higher levels of Lin28a and lower let-7 activity.
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data described in the text.

claim: Expansion of the Wnt niche prevents silencing of early neural crest factors Pax7 and FoxD3.
source: The expansion of the Wnt niche also prevents silencing of early neural crest factors Pax7 and FoxD3 (Figure 5m).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5m.

claim: Maintenance of stem identity by Wnt gain-of-function results in suppression of differentiation.
source: Furthermore, this maintenance of stem identity resulted in suppression of differentiation, as Wnt gain-of-function resulted in lower expression levels of drivers of ectomenchymal differentiation Runx2, Alx1, and Barx2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2a–b).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2a-b.

claim: Manipulation of the Wnt-Lin28a/let-7 regulatory circuit impacts both progenitor identity and the onset of differentiation.
source: These findings show that manipulation of the Wnt-Lin28a/let-7 regulatory circuit impacts both progenitor identity and the onset of differentiation, indicating that this mechanism controls the transition between these two states.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the Wnt manipulation experiments.

claim: A regulatory circuit formed by Wnt, Lin28a and let-7 miRNAs controls the deployment and the subsequent silencing of the multipotency program in a position-dependent manner.
source: Our results show that a regulatory circuit formed by Wnt, Lin28a and let-7 miRNAs controls the deployment and the subsequent silencing of the multipotency program in a position-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings.

claim: Transition from multipotency to differentiation is determined by the topological relationship between the migratory cells and the dorsal neural tube, which acts as a Wnt-producing stem cell niche.
source: Transition from multipotency to differentiation is determined by the topological relationship between the migratory cells and the dorsal neural tube, which acts as a Wnt-producing stem cell niche.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings.

claim: High levels of Wnt ligands produced by the dorsal neural tube activate Lin28a transcription in neural crest stem cells.
source: According to our model (Figure 5n), high levels of Wnt ligands produced by the dorsal neural tube activate Lin28a transcription in neural crest stem cells.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model shown in Figure 5n.

claim: High levels of Lin28a inhibit let-7 activity, protecting the neural crest transcriptional network from repression by these miRNAs.
source: The high levels of the Lin28a in turn inhibit let-7 activity, protecting the neural crest transcriptional network from repression by these miRNAs.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model.

claim: As neural crest cells migrate away from the Wnt source, Lin28a levels are significantly reduced, resulting in an increase of mature let-7 levels and subsequent repression of multipotency factors.
source: As neural crest cells migrate away from the Wnt source, Lin28a levels are significantly reduced, resulting in an increase of mature let-7 levels and subsequent repression of multipotency factors.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model.

claim: Inhibition of crucial network nodes by let-7 results in silencing of the neural crest gene regulatory network and loss of stem cell identity.
source: This inhibition of crucial network nodes results in silencing of the neural crest gene regulatory network and loss of stem cell identity.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model.

claim: Canonical Wnt signaling acts via the Lin28a/let-7 axis to promote neural crest multipotency.
source: Our results indicate that canonical Wnt signaling acts via the Lin28a/let-7 axis to promote neural crest multipotency.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data.

claim: The dorsal neural tube is an important signaling center in the embryo, acting to maintain neural crest stem cells in a multipotent state.
source: Our results indicate that the dorsal neural tube is an important signaling center in the embryo, acting to maintain neural crest stem cells in a multipotent state.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data.

claim: Lin28a and its paralog, Lin28b, are dynamically expressed during amniote embryonic development.
source: Little was known about the role of Lin28a in neural crest development before our analysis; previous work showed that Lin28a and its paralog, Lin28b, are dynamically expressed during amniote embryonic development (Yokoyama et al., 2008), and in vitro experiments suggest that these factors play a role in neurogliogenesis (Balzer et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In vitro experiments suggest that Lin28a and Lin28b play a role in neurogliogenesis.
source: Little was known about the role of Lin28a in neural crest development before our analysis; previous work showed that Lin28a and its paralog, Lin28b, are dynamically expressed during amniote embryonic development (Yokoyama et al., 2008), and in vitro experiments suggest that these factors play a role in neurogliogenesis (Balzer et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Balzer et al., 2010.

claim: Lin28a is a regulator of pluripotency in stem cells and cancer.
source: Here we identify an essential function of Lin28a factor during the early stages neural crest development, which is consistent with its role as a regulator of pluripotency in stem cells and cancer (Shyh-Chang and Daley, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Shyh-Chang and Daley, 2013.

claim: The regulatory mechanism involving Wnt-Lin28a/let-7 is independent of the role of Wnts in neural crest induction and specification.
source: We postulate that this regulatory mechanism is independent of the role of Wnts in neural crest induction and specification (Simões-Costa et al., 2015; García-Castro et al., 2002), and its later function as a driver of differentiation into melanocytes (Dorsky et al., 1998) and sensory neurons (Lee et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a postulated claim supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Neural crest cells display specific responses to Wnt manipulations performed at distinct stages of development.
source: Neural crest cells display specific responses to Wnt manipulations performed at distinct stages of development, both before (Simões-Costa et al., 2015; García-Castro et al., 2002) and after specification (Hari et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Timing of intracellular response to Wnt signaling is crucial for specificity.
source: While we still have a limited understanding of the mechanisms that compartmentalize the distinct functions of the pathway, time-controlled studies have shown that timing of intracellular response is crucial for specificity (Hari et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hari et al., 2012.

claim: Lin28 activation by Wnts is established very early in neural crest progenitors and this interaction is lost as the response to the pathway is attenuated during migration.
source: Our results suggest that Lin28 activation by Wnts is established very early in neural crest progenitors and that this interaction is lost as the response to the pathway is attenuated during migration.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data.

claim: In birds, neural crest cells form two waves of migration, with the melanocytic subpopulation delaminating later than the chondrocytic and neural progenitors.
source: In birds, neural crest cells form two waves of migration, with the melanocytic subpopulation delaminating later than the chondrocytic and neural progenitors (Erickson and Goins, 1995; Le Douarin and Kalcheim, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Studies in the neural crest gene network have revealed numerous positive interactions that act to stabilize progenitor cell identity.
source: Studies in the neural crest gene network have revealed numerous positive interactions that act to stabilize progenitor cell identity (Simões-Costa and Bronner, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Simões-Costa and Bronner, 2015.

claim: The presence of positive regulatory loops is a common feature of developmental regulatory networks.
source: Indeed, the presence of positive regulatory loops is a common feature of developmental regulatory networks (Davidson, 2010; Davidson and Levine, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Davidson, 2010 and Davidson and Levine, 2008.

claim: The majority of the components of the neural crest gene regulatory network are only transiently expressed, being downregulated as the cells migrate away from the neural tube.
source: This rapid silencing of progenitor identity during differentiation is evident in our quantitative analysis (Figure 1d), which shows that the majority of the components of the network are only transiently expressed, being downregulated as the cells migrate away from the neural tube.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Pax3/7 has been shown to activate itself to stabilize and maintain neural crest identity.
source: For instance Pax3/7 has been shown to activate itself to stabilize and maintain neural crest identity (Plouhinec et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Plouhinec et al., 2014.

claim: Tfap2a, Sox9 and Snai2 form a positive feedback loop in neural crest cells.
source: Similarly, Tfap2a, Sox9 and Snai2 form a positive feedback loop in neural crest cells, (Luo et al., 2003) which may explain the rapid increase in expression of these factors during neural crest specification.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Luo et al., 2003.

claim: SoxE factors partake in auto-regulatory loops in multiple contexts.
source: SoxE factors are also known to partake and auto-regulatory loops in multiple contexts (Mead et al., 2013; O'Donnell et al., 2006; Honoré et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In the absence of Lin28a, the expression of mature let-7 microRNAs increases dramatically, reaching levels sufficient to inhibit neural crest stem cell identity.
source: Our experiments indicate that in the absence of Lin28a, the expression of mature let-7 microRNAs increases dramatically (Figure 3c–e), reaching levels that are sufficient to inhibit neural crest stem cell identity.
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR and sensor data shown in Figures 3c-e.

claim: The let-7 target genes identified in the UTR-reporter assay represent critical nodes of the network that are involved in the regulation of multiple neural crest genes.
source: This is due to the fact that the let-7 target genes identified in our UTR-reporter assay represent critical nodes of the network that are involved in the regulation of multiple neural crest genes (Simões-Costa and Bronner, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the UTR-reporter data and a citation to Simões-Costa and Bronner, 2015.

claim: Pax3/7, FoxD3 and cMyc are stem cell factors and bona fide markers of neural crest cells, which play central roles in induction and specification.
source: Pax3/7, FoxD3 and cMyc are stem cell factors and bona fide markers of neural crest cells, which play central roles in induction and specification (Dottori et al., 2001; Krishnakumar et al., 2016; Basch et al., 2006; Kerosuo and Bronner, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Pax3/7, FoxD3 and cMyc are part of a group of genes that define neural crest stem cell identity located within the Wnt niche.
source: These factors are also part of a group of genes that define neural crest stem cell identity (Lignell et al., 2017) located within the Wnt niche.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lignell et al., 2017.

claim: A Wnt-Lin28a/let-7 regulatory circuit is able to modulate the neural crest regulatory program.
source: Our demonstration that a Wnt-Lin28a/let-7 regulatory circuit is able to modulate this regulatory program highlights how gene networks can be extensively remodeled during cell state transitions.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data.
